For some reason, it appears as though smaller plants can tolerate much warmer temps. than larger plants, lots of people have experienced the same thing.


Completely agreed! My biggest plant is a dual growth point XL ( by Phil G's standards) took an absolute beating last year once the temps started rising. That plant is capable of over 2 foot pitchers. As you can see the little guys took the heat with a grain of salt. This year I'll be cutting back the direct sun to all of my cobras to about 5-6 hours of morning sun to try and beat the heat instead of letting the heat beat my plants.


AudacityOfTheMind. I did a four week strat on one batch of about 30 seeds split between two sources. I had one seed sprout. I did an 8 week strat oon the second batch and now I have an army.

posts.body_html: I've been keeping a foot tall cobra in a 90 gallon terrarium with my cephalotus for about 3 months. Temps never get above 80F and at night they drop to 63F. Also, as the lights go out every night, I flush the cobra pot with refrigerated water that's at about 38F to 42F. I know this isn't really sustainable since the plant will surely outgrow the tank, but under the LEDs it's growing relatively slowly (though with good color), so I may have a couple more years with it yet. Once it gets too big, maybe 1.5 or 2 feet tall, I think I'm going to try to grow it in a big east facing window. I've killed them before, experimenting with outdoor growing here in Alabama, and if I kill this one, I think that'll be the end of cobras for me. I really like them, but damn are they picky.

posts.body_html:
Maybe the fact that most of the warmer climate countries kept their water cool while keeping it in big ceramic amphorae or other open pored containers would help to solve your problem.

Evaporating heat loss is not that difficult. I have built myself such containers out of ceramic material. You only have to provide enough water supply with little mineral content to keep the plant roots cool and happy.

You could even build a shadowed area with a chimney (stack effect) connected, where the air is always moving along the ceramic structure which lies in the shadow of a table with holes where they stand in. Or a solar powered fan to move the air.
A float switch will provide always fresh water.

If you don’t understand what I want to say I can make a quick draft to show the construction.
Insulation has its limits, this solution will work in long heat periods with little energy input.

May 20, 2013 1:22:45 GMT -5 meizzwang said:
Here's a bunch of cobra plants that I've grown from seeds. These take a VERY long time to grow under my conditions because during the summer, these hang out in the shade. Shade=slower growth. During the end of fall until we get our first hot days, these are blasted with full sun, and they love it. We had a heat wave over 90F a few weeks ago, and surprisingly, they didn't get stressed out. Cool nights are key to keeping them happy.

Okay, done rambling, on with the photos!

All pics taken 5/19/13-check out how spooky this one looks!





Shallow tray of cobras-as seedlings, they don't seem to mind not having deep soil:









I've had mixed success growing these in trays like this-they either thrive, or all perish! still learning how to keep these things happy:



That Moss you have Mike is a few years old yes? I have sphagnum from 1975 and it is like 1 ft deep or more. When the Moss gets old it looks like a 1970s shaggy carpet lol! Is that North Carolina sphag Moss Mike? Nice colony you have👍
